title: 1 Samuel 7:5–14
context: Samuel tells all Israel to gather to Mizpah, and he will pray to the LORD for them. They gather, draw water and pour it out before the LORD, fast that day, and confess, “We have sinned against the LORD.” Samuel judged the children of Israel in Mizpah. When the Philistines hear of the gathering, their lords go up against Israel, and Israel is afraid. The people plead with Samuel not to stop crying to the LORD their God for them, that he will save them out of the Philistines’ hand. Samuel offers a suckling lamb as a whole burnt offering, cries to the LORD for Israel, and the LORD answers him. As he is offering, the Philistines draw near; but the LORD thunders with a great thunder that day, confuses them, and they are struck down before Israel. Israel pursues them as far as Beth Kar. Samuel then sets a stone between Mizpah and Shen, and names it Ebenezer, saying, “The LORD helped us until now.” The Philistines are subdued and stop coming within Israel’s border; the LORD’s hand is against them all the days of Samuel. The cities the Philistines had taken are restored, from Ekron even to Gath, the border is recovered, and there is peace between Israel and the Amorites. Both traditions read the unit as repentance joined to the LORD’s help. The name Ebenezer marks that help. The poured water is a rite whose exact meaning is discussed (a sign of pouring out the heart, a libation of repentance, or a symbolic emptying); those are options, not a consensus, and not a contrast between the two traditions.

verses.text: Samuel said, “Gather all Israel to Mizpah, and I will pray to the LORD for you.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Samuel said, “Gather all Israel to Mizpah, and I will pray to the LORD for you.” The return of verses 3–4 is now given a public place and an intercessor.

Arminian readers hear a real summons and a real promise to pray. All Israel is to gather; Samuel will pray to the LORD for them. The next verses will show them coming, and him praying.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same gathering and the same prayer. Mizpah, as the WEB spells it, becomes the place where the people will confess and where Samuel will cry to the LORD.

Both traditions take the verse as the call to assembly and intercession, shared ground before the confession of verse 6.

verses.text: They gathered together to Mizpah, and drew water, and poured it out before the LORD, and fasted on that day, and said there, “We have sinned against the LORD.” Samuel judged the children of Israel in Mizpah.
verses.arminianNotes:
They gathered together to Mizpah, and drew water, and poured it out before the LORD, and fasted on that day, and said there, “We have sinned against the LORD.” Samuel judged the children of Israel in Mizpah.

Arminian readers hear a confession that matches the putting away of the gods in verse 4. They fast, they say they have sinned, and Samuel judges them there. The poured water is a rite whose precise meaning is not explained; readers have suggested a pouring out of the heart, a libation of repentance, or a sign of emptying, and none of those should be treated as a settled consensus.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the gathering, the fasting, and the spoken confession as the heart of the scene, with Samuel judging Israel at Mizpah. The water poured out before the LORD belongs to that penitence; its exact symbolism is discussed rather than proved.

Both traditions read “We have sinned against the LORD” as shared ground of repentance, and they refuse to turn the water rite into a party dispute.

verses.text: When the Philistines heard that the children of Israel were gathered together at Mizpah, the lords of the Philistines went up against Israel. When the children of Israel heard it, they were afraid of the Philistines.
verses.arminianNotes:
When the Philistines heard that the children of Israel were gathered together at Mizpah, the lords of the Philistines went up against Israel. When the children of Israel heard it, they were afraid of the Philistines.

Arminian readers hear how quickly the assembly is tested. Repentance has not made the enemy vanish; the lords come up, and Israel is genuinely afraid. The next verse will show where they take that fear.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the Philistine advance is a response to the gathering at Mizpah, and that Israel’s fear is real. The LORD’s help, still to be asked and given, has not yet appeared in thunder.

Both traditions take the verse as the crisis that drives the people to plead for prayer, shared narrative ground, not a contrast over the military situation.

verses.text: The children of Israel said to Samuel, “Don’t stop crying to the LORD our God for us, that he will save us out of the hand of the Philistines.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The children of Israel said to Samuel, “Don’t stop crying to the LORD our God for us, that he will save us out of the hand of the Philistines.” They want his intercession to continue, and they want the LORD to save.

Arminian readers hear a people now asking for salvation from God, not first from their own arms. They call him “the LORD our God”, and they beg Samuel not to stop crying to him. The request is urgent and sincere.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the plea as faith seeking the LORD’s salvation through a prophet’s cry. The help they want is that “he will save us out of the hand of the Philistines”, the very deliverance promised in verse 3.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground: salvation is asked of the LORD, and Samuel’s crying to him is the means they cling to in their fear.

verses.text: Samuel took a suckling lamb, and offered it for a whole burnt offering to the LORD. Samuel cried to the LORD for Israel, and the LORD answered him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Samuel took a suckling lamb, and offered it for a whole burnt offering to the LORD. Samuel cried to the LORD for Israel, and the LORD answered him.

Arminian readers hear both the offering and the cry, and then a real answer. The LORD answered him: the prayer is not left hanging, and the next verse will show how that answer meets the approaching army.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that Samuel’s cry is for Israel, and that the answer is the LORD’s. The suckling lamb as a whole burnt offering and the prophet’s voice are the means; the response is God’s.

Both traditions take the verse as intercession heard, shared ground of the LORD’s help already stated before the thunder is described.

verses.text: As Samuel was offering up the burnt offering, the Philistines came near to battle against Israel; but the LORD thundered with a great thunder on that day on the Philistines and confused them; and they were struck down before Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
As Samuel was offering up the burnt offering, the Philistines came near to battle against Israel; but the LORD thundered with a great thunder on that day on the Philistines and confused them; and they were struck down before Israel.

Arminian readers hear the LORD’s own intervention at the very moment of the offering and of the enemy’s approach. Israel does not strike first. A great thunder confuses the Philistines, and they are struck down before Israel. The help is his.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the “but”: the Philistines come near, and the LORD thunders. The confusion and the striking down are his work on that day, while the burnt offering is still being offered.

Both traditions read the verse as the LORD’s direct help in battle, shared ground, the act that the stone in verse 12 will name.

verses.text: The men of Israel went out of Mizpah and pursued the Philistines, and struck them until they came under Beth Kar.
verses.arminianNotes:
The men of Israel went out of Mizpah and pursued the Philistines, and struck them until they came under Beth Kar. The people take up a pursuit the LORD has already broken open.

Arminian readers hear a real following-through. They go out of Mizpah and strike as far as Beth Kar, a place the text names and does not further locate. The victory is pursued, not left unused.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the pursuit as Israel’s part after the thunder. The LORD has confused the enemy; the men of Israel now strike them as far as Beth Kar.

Both traditions read the verse as the human sequel to God’s intervention, shared ground, without inventing a settled site for Beth Kar.

verses.text: Then Samuel took a stone and set it between Mizpah and Shen, and called its name Ebenezer, saying, “The LORD helped us until now.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Then Samuel took a stone and set it between Mizpah and Shen, and called its name Ebenezer, saying, “The LORD helped us until now.” The stone is a memorial of help, placed between two named points.

Arminian readers hear Samuel teaching the people how to remember the day. The name and the sentence are one: the LORD helped them until now. An earlier Ebenezer in this book marked a place of defeat when the ark was lost; whether this stone reclaims that memory or stands as a new marker between Mizpah and Shen is discussed, and should not be treated as a settled identification.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same confession: “The LORD helped us until now.” The help is dated—“until now”—and set in stone, so that the victory is referred to the LORD and not to Israel’s pursuit alone.

Both traditions take Ebenezer as shared ground of the LORD’s help, the heart of these two chapters, without forcing a contrast over the earlier place of that name.

verses.text: So the Philistines were subdued, and they stopped coming within the border of Israel. The LORD’s hand was against the Philistines all the days of Samuel.
verses.arminianNotes:
So the Philistines were subdued, and they stopped coming within the border of Israel. “The LORD’s hand was against the Philistines all the days of Samuel.” The help of verse 12 is given a lasting frame in Samuel’s time.

Arminian readers hear a real restraint of the enemy through the days of this judge and prophet. The border holds because the LORD’s hand is against them, not because Israel has become invincible on its own.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that it is the LORD’s hand, all the days of Samuel, that keeps the Philistines from coming within the border. The later wars of other reigns are not this verse’s subject; the narrator is describing Samuel’s period.

Both traditions take the verse as the enduring help of the LORD in Samuel’s days, shared ground with the name Ebenezer.

verses.text: The cities which the Philistines had taken from Israel were restored to Israel, from Ekron even to Gath; and Israel recovered its border out of the hand of the Philistines. There was peace between Israel and the Amorites.
verses.arminianNotes:
The cities which the Philistines had taken from Israel were restored to Israel, from Ekron even to Gath; and Israel recovered its border out of the hand of the Philistines. There was peace between Israel and the Amorites.

Arminian readers hear the fruit of the LORD’s help in restored towns and a recovered border, and in peace with the Amorites as well. The line “from Ekron even to Gath” is the narrator’s way of marking that recovery; it need not be turned into a detailed map beyond what the verse says.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the restoration, the recovered border, and the peace with the Amorites as the outworking of the LORD’s hand in verses 10–13. What had been lost to the Philistines is given back in this period.

Both traditions read the verse as the earthly fruit of the help already confessed at Ebenezer, shared ground, without a contrast over the later fortunes of those cities.
